Inimical

ih-NIM-ih-kul · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Inimical is harmful or hostile, especially in relation to something else.

The new zoning law was seen as inimical to the neighborhood's small, family-owned shops.

Worked Example

Doctors warned that skipping meals entirely is inimical to long-term metabolic health.

Skipping meals doesn't just fail to help -- it actively works against the body's health, which is exactly inimical.

How Inimical Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

hostile

hostile: actively unfriendly or opposed

antagonistic

antagonistic: showing active opposition or dislike

Antonyms

favorable

favorable: helpful and encouraging toward something

How Strong Is It? — unhelpful → destructive → inimical

unhelpful vs. inimical

unhelpful vs. inimical: Something unhelpful simply fails to assist; something inimical actively works against the thing it touches.

destructive vs. inimical

destructive vs. inimical: Inimical describes an ongoing harmful relationship between two things; destructive implies the harm has already caused serious damage.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root — imic

root — imic: friend (Latin (amicus))

suffix — -al

suffix — -al: relating to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Inimical comes from Latin in- ('not') + amicus ('friend') + -al -- literally 'not friendly.'

Use the root in a new word: enemy

Use the root in a new word: enemy: That same Latin root, by way of Old French, gives us the everyday word enemy -- inimical and enemy are word-family cousins.

Root Check

Word Choice

Inimical almost always pairs with "to" (inimical to health, inimical to progress), describing a harmful relationship rather than a standalone quality, distinct from this unit's Baneful, which can describe a harmful thing on its own.
